title: Teacher shortages expose education as a social-infrastructure and status bargain
source_unit: OECD, Education at a Glance 2026: OECD Indicators, 2026
geography: OECD countries and partner economies, with detailed teacher-shortage indicators for participating education systems

observations.period: 2024/25 school year; teacher supply and shortage conditions across OECD education systems

qualification_gap.unit: percent of primary and secondary teachers not fully qualified

attrition.unit: percent of fully qualified primary and secondary teachers who left during the school year

distribution.value: shortages are more acute in rural, remote and disadvantaged communities and concentrated in mathematics and natural sciences

mechanism.value: education quality becomes geographically and socially unequal when a common system relies on unequal access to qualified teachers

observations.method: Internationally comparable OECD education indicators, teacher-shortage data collection, and Teaching and Learning International Survey evidence, supplemented by country-level administrative reporting.
observations.uncertainty: Vacancy, qualification, absence, attrition and satisfaction measures are not identical across countries; unfilled positions are only one manifestation of shortage and cross-country comparisons require methodological caution.
observations.subgroup: Students and families in remote, rural and disadvantaged communities; learners needing mathematics and science instruction; non-fully-qualified teachers; and schools competing for scarce specialist staff.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher non-qualification shares can reflect alternative certification or entry pathways rather than uniformly lower teaching quality; observed shortages may also reflect local labor-market, demographic or reporting differences.

observations.period: 2024; teacher work experience, recognition and recruitment conditions

job_satisfaction.unit: percent of teachers reporting job satisfaction

social_recognition.unit: percent of teachers who believe teaching is valued by society

terms_and_pay.value: 68% of lower-secondary teachers report satisfaction with employment terms excluding salary, while 39% report salary satisfaction

mechanism.value: retention and recruitment depend not only on pay but also on workload, autonomy, school climate, relationships, leadership, career development and public status

observations.method: OECD teacher-shortage indicators and TALIS 2024 survey evidence on lower-secondary teachers’ working conditions, satisfaction and perceptions of social value.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported cross-sectional associations and do not establish which condition causes entry, retention or exit; satisfaction and public recognition may be shaped by country-specific institutional and cultural context.
observations.subgroup: Teachers, prospective entrants, students and parents, school leaders, mid-career professionals, and communities that depend on stable school relationships.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public recognition may be an outcome of broader working conditions or media narratives rather than an independent retention lever; raising status without reducing workload or improving pay may not change supply.

observations.period: 2024–2033; demographic change, teacher careers and qualification value

denominator.unit: OECD projection and comparative labor-market frame

demographic_shift.unit: percent projected change in the OECD population aged 5–14 between 2024 and 2033

ageing_workforce.unit: percent of OECD secondary teachers aged 55 or older

second_career.unit: percent of lower-secondary teachers who are second-career entrants

qualification_uncertainty.value: between 2023 and 2025, unemployment among tertiary-educated 25–34 year-olds rose 0.4 percentage points while it fell 0.2 points among those with upper-secondary attainment

mechanism.value: declining student numbers do not automatically relieve shortages because demographic change, retirement, regional allocation, career mobility and changing returns to qualifications must be coordinated

observations.method: OECD demographic projections, education workforce indicators, second-career teacher measures and labor-market indicators by educational attainment.
observations.uncertainty: The qualification-employment divergence is a short recent period and the report says it is too early to determine whether it is temporary or a lasting shift; projections are conditional and do not predict local school closures or staffing outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Older teachers approaching retirement, mid-career entrants, young tertiary graduates, students in shrinking or growing regions, and communities affected by teacher reallocation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower enrolment could create fiscal and staffing room if systems reallocate effectively; a short-term rise in tertiary-educated unemployment does not demonstrate a structural collapse in the value of higher education or an AI-driven shift.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD publication page with key figures, teacher-shortage findings, metadata and country coverage.
Official DOI for Education at a Glance 2026.

boundary: This record identifies teacher supply as a social-infrastructure and status problem: unequal staffing, working conditions, public recognition, demographic change and labor-market competition shape the stability of education access. It is comparative indicator and survey evidence, not causal proof that any single salary, AI, second-career or reallocation policy improves learning, retention, equity or social trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD PDF and publication page, teacher-shortage key figures, spatial and subject distribution, qualification and attrition measures, satisfaction and recognition contrasts, second-career pathways, demographic projections, and recent qualification-employment divergence were reviewed.
